cards.title: Forecast Transactional Repeat Customers with a 6-Month Rolling Return Rate
cards.summary: Estimate how many one-time buyers return each month by applying a measured return rate to the trailing six months of acquired customers.
cards.use_when: Modeling repeat revenue and LTV for non-subscription customers where you cannot simply use 1/churn.

cards.title: Compute Subscription Lifetime Orders from Monthly Churn
cards.summary: Estimate lifetime subscription orders from billed periods, order frequency and contribution per shipment.
cards.use_when: Comparing subscriber versus one-time-buyer value to decide how hard to push subscription conversion and how much you can afford to spend acquiring subscribers.

cards.title: Report Post-Marketing Contribution Margin as the Core Profitability Gauge
cards.summary: Track contribution margin minus marketing each month to know whether the store can fund payroll and overhead at all.
cards.use_when: Monthly P&L review or investor reporting for any ecommerce store, especially when early customers are heavily first-time buyers.

cards.title: Build a Simple Bucketed Payroll and Opex Forecast
cards.summary: Forecast people costs by functional bucket and headcount, then layer non-payroll opex to reach operating income.
cards.use_when: Building or updating a store's operating expense forecast and finding the month where operating income turns positive.

cards.title: Model tax losses separately from book losses and cash tax payments
cards.summary: Keep tax-loss assumptions explicit when forecasting cash for a store approaching profitability.
cards.use_when: Cash planning and investor communications for an unprofitable-early store that is turning profitable, to avoid over-forecasting tax outflows.

cards.title: Forecast Inventory with Lead Time and Cycle Time Before You Model Cash
cards.summary: Work out when to place purchase orders by pairing supplier lead time with expected sell-through cycle, then cost each PO.
cards.use_when: Replenishment planning for any physical-product store to avoid stockouts and to see the true cash hit of inventory buys.

cards.title: Build a Mini Cash Flow Statement to Find Working Capital Needs and Runway
cards.summary: Reconcile net income with inventory purchases to project real cash burn and how much capital the store must raise.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much funding or cash buffer the store needs and when, especially for inventory-heavy CPG or subscription-box businesses.

cards.title: Gross Revenue to Net Revenue Bridge: Report Refunds and Discounts Separately
cards.summary: Show gross revenue, then refunds/returns, then discounts, then net revenue — and split net revenue between first-time and repeat customers.
cards.use_when: Designing the monthly reporting pack or income statement presentation so you can see how much revenue discounts and refunds consume.

cards.title: Reconcile Your Model: Gross Profit Percentage Must Match Unit Economics
cards.summary: Use the gross profit rate as an arithmetic check that every revenue and COGS line is forecast correctly.
cards.use_when: After building or editing a financial model, before presenting numbers to investors or using them for decisions.

cards.title: Consolidate Segments and Report the Ecommerce KPI Set
cards.summary: Roll transactional and subscription segments into one business view and report a fixed monthly KPI set to spot direction, not just level.
cards.use_when: Monthly management or investor reporting for a mixed one-time/subscription store; setting which numbers get tracked every month.

cards.title: Churn rate only applies to subscriptions — use retention for one-off stores
cards.summary: Churn rate measures the share of subscription customers who cancel in a period; non-subscription ecommerce must use cohort retention instead.
cards.use_when: Choosing which metric to track for a subscription box, replenishment program or membership versus a one-off direct-to-consumer catalog.

cards.title: Calculate churn against the prior period's base, not the current month
cards.summary: Churn = cancellations in a period divided by subscriptions at the start of that period, because cancellations happen at renewal from the prior cohort.
cards.use_when: Reporting or setting targets for monthly churn on a subscription store, and auditing any churn number a team or agency has provided.

cards.title: Convert churn into average customer lifetime with 1/churn
cards.summary: Average customer lifetime equals 1 divided by the churn rate over the same period, which lets you compare monthly and annual subscriptions on one scale.
cards.use_when: Comparing payback and LTV scenarios across subscription plans, renewal frequencies or box programs when you need a common lifetime figure in months.

cards.title: Build a cohort retention table as the only valid retention view
cards.summary: Organize customers by first-purchase month and track the same group forward; do not try to read retention from aggregate monthly totals.
cards.use_when: Setting up retention reporting for a subscription or repeat-purchase store, or evaluating a data/analytics tool purchase for the store.

cards.title: Track net revenue retention separately from customer retention
cards.summary: Build a revenue-by-cohort table so you can see whether surviving customers spend more or less over time, not just how many remain.
cards.use_when: Assessing a subscription store where add-ons, upsells, box upgrades or price changes are meant to lift revenue per customer over time.

cards.title: Derive customer lifetime value per cohort in three columns
cards.summary: Cumulative lifetime revenue divided by the original cohort size, multiplied by gross margin, gives the LTV you should actually set CAC against.
cards.use_when: Setting the maximum allowable customer acquisition cost for a subscription or replenishment offer, or stress-testing a media plan's breakeven.

cards.title: Calculate CAC payback from cohorts, not from flat monthly gross profit
cards.summary: Dividing CAC by a single month's gross profit ignores churn; real payback must sum declining cohort gross profit until cumulative profit covers CAC.
cards.use_when: Deciding how fast a subscription or replenishment offer repays acquisition spend before scaling the media budget.

cards.title: Inspect what survives after payback, not just whether you break even
cards.summary: Two cohorts can both repay CAC while only one generates meaningful profit afterward, so read the tail of the cohort, not the breakeven date alone.
cards.use_when: Comparing subscription offers, pricing tiers or market segments before committing incremental media budget, or deciding whether to reprice a program.

cards.title: Choose subscription-compatible products and structure the offer
cards.summary: Subscriptions work for consumables and continuous needs; the recurring cadence, skippability and bundling of the offer drive the metrics.
cards.use_when: Selecting which SKUs to put on subscription or replenishment, and configuring cadence, bundles or memberships before launch.

cards.title: Recognize the churn-driven hurdles subscription boxes face with investors
cards.summary: High churn plus heavy acquisition spend makes subscription physical-goods stores hard to fund; sharp unit economics and retention data are what overcome it.
cards.use_when: Preparing a subscription store for fundraising, a board update or an internal go/no-go decision on scaling spend.

cards.title: Convert monthly and annual churn on a consistent survival basis
cards.summary: Normalize subscription churn through retained-customer survival before comparing rates.
cards.use_when: Comparing retention between plans or channels with different billing frequencies, or reviewing a subscription store's dashboard with mixed units.

cards.title: Read one calendar month diagonally across the cohort table
cards.summary: A single month's total revenue comes from many cohorts at different relationship ages, so totals hide which cohort is deteriorating.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing a revenue or order decline on a subscription store when top-line reporting looks stable, or reviewing a monthly performance deck.

cards.title: Build the cohort model in a spreadsheet with locked denominators
cards.summary: The cohort, cumulative revenue and LTV tables come from a small set of formulas with an absolute column reference to the original cohort size.
cards.use_when: Standing up repeatable retention and LTV reporting for a subscription store without waiting on engineering resources.

cards.title: Unit economics first: profit per order before anything else
cards.summary: Break down a single order's price, costs and gross margin before evaluating growth or marketing spend.
cards.use_when: You are launching or auditing a subscription box or physical product and need to know whether the business can make money per order before scaling ads.

cards.title: Use churn-rate lifetime as a fast fallback, not the real answer
cards.summary: A quick LTV approximation from churn rate and gross profit per order, useful only when you have no cohort data.
cards.use_when: You have a new subscription store with almost no retention history and need a rough LTV for early ad spend decisions.

cards.title: Read a retention cohort table to calculate lifetime revenue
cards.summary: Organize repeat purchases by signup month to see true retention, cumulative revenue and profit-based LTV over time.
cards.use_when: You have several months of subscription or repeat-purchase data and need a defensible customer lifetime value for ad budget decisions.

cards.title: Blended vs paid CAC: calculate both and know why
cards.summary: Split acquisition cost into blended (all spend / all new customers) and paid-only (ad spend / paid-attributed new customers) to judge whether growth is scalable.
cards.use_when: You run paid ads plus organic channels and need to decide whether you can profitably increase ad budget.

cards.title: Interpret the LTV:CAC ratio with the source's heuristics
cards.summary: Ratio of lifetime gross profit to acquisition cost signals whether the store can self-fund growth or needs outside capital.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to raise ad spend aggressively, seek investment, or fix retention/COGS first.

cards.title: Lever 1: Raise LTV by cutting churn and adding pause options
cards.summary: Small reductions in monthly churn have the largest single effect on lifetime value for subscription stores.
cards.use_when: Your LTV:CAC ratio is thin and you are looking for the highest-leverage place to improve subscription economics.

cards.title: Lever 2: Raise AOV without competing on price
cards.summary: Upsells, tiers and value-based branding raise revenue per order and improve LTV.
cards.use_when: You want to raise LTV per subscriber without finding entirely new customers.

cards.title: Lever 3: Renegotiate COGS as volume grows
cards.summary: Product, fulfillment and shipping costs all fall with scale, increasing LTV without changing price or retention.
cards.use_when: You have grown order volume and want to convert scale into higher lifetime value and contribution margin.

cards.title: Decide how long a window to use for LTV
cards.summary: Choose an observation window by finding the point where cumulative cohort revenue stops meaningfully increasing.
cards.use_when: You need to fix a defensible LTV horizon for budgeting or investor conversations, especially for non-subscription or seasonal stores.

cards.title: Model paid Amazon launch orders and uncertain organic follow-on sales
cards.summary: Assess launch advertising against contribution and a conservative organic-sales scenario.
cards.use_when: You are launching a physical product on Amazon and deciding how much to lose on early ad-driven sales.

cards.title: Model lifetime orders per customer before committing ad budget
cards.summary: Estimate how many times a customer repurchases to convert first-order profit into true lifetime value.
cards.use_when: You sell a consumable product and need to justify acquisition spend above first-order margin.

cards.title: Sequence the forecast from marketing spend forward
cards.summary: Forecast ecommerce financials by starting with marketing budget, converting it to orders via CAC, then deriving inventory and cash needs.
cards.use_when: You are building a financial model for a new ecommerce or Amazon FBA business and need to know how much inventory and cash to line up.

cards.title: Subscription retention benchmarking lesson from Dollar Shave Club
cards.summary: High long-tail retention, not high first-month retention, made a low-AOV subscription valuable.
cards.use_when: You are evaluating or building a low-price subscription and need to understand what makes the model worth investing in.

cards.title: Build an Amazon FBA order forecast from marketing spend
cards.summary: Model paid orders from a monthly marketing budget divided by CAC, then layer a paid-to-organic ratio that grows as reviews accumulate.
cards.use_when: You are planning a new Amazon FBA product launch or replenishment cycle and need a 12-18 month order forecast before deciding how much inventory to buy and how much cash to raise.

cards.title: Model inventory timing with a lead-time lag row
cards.summary: Offset inventory purchases by the supplier lead time so the model shows when stock actually arrives and when you go negative.
cards.use_when: You are building or auditing a cash model for a physical product where stock is bought months before it can be sold.

cards.title: Forecast inventory funding gaps with a monthly cash bridge
cards.summary: Separate units-sold profit from supplier-payment timing to find when an ecommerce store needs cash.
cards.use_when: You have an order and inventory forecast and need to quantify the funding gap before committing to a launch or a scaling plan.

cards.title: Evaluate non-dilutive inventory and marketing financing
cards.summary: Revenue-share financing lets you fund inventory without selling equity, repaid as a percentage of revenue plus a flat fee.
cards.use_when: Your cash model shows a funding gap for inventory or paid acquisition and you are weighing equity dilution against revenue-based financing.

cards.title: Calculate customer lifetime value from churn and gross margin
cards.summary: Estimate subscription contribution LTV using consistent monthly purchase frequency, margin and churn, then validate against observed cohorts.
cards.use_when: You are setting a CAC ceiling for a subscription or repeat-purchase store and need to know how much you can afford to spend to acquire one customer.

cards.title: Spend above first-order profit when LTV justifies it
cards.summary: A subscription can profitably spend more on acquisition than the first order returns because later months repay the CAC.
cards.use_when: You are deciding whether to scale paid acquisition on a subscription product even though first-order economics look unprofitable.

cards.title: Model discounts and CAC as one combined acquisition cost
cards.summary: A discount and paid acquisition are mathematically equivalent spend per customer — add them together to see true cost of acquisition.
cards.use_when: You are choosing between a deeper discount and more ad spend to drive first purchases and want to compare them on equal footing.

cards.title: Choose the discount/CAC mix that maximises total contribution margin
cards.summary: Compare scenarios on total revenue and total post-marketing contribution margin, not on per-customer margin alone.
cards.use_when: You are setting a promotional calendar or ad budget and deciding whether a bigger discount can be offset by higher volume.

cards.title: Attach your best discounts to a loyalty or subscription on-ramp
cards.summary: Give the deepest discounts in exchange for enrolling in a subscription or loyalty program rather than as a flash sale.
cards.use_when: You are designing the offer and landing page for a promotion and deciding whether the discount should require a commitment.

cards.title: Build a Daily Contribution Margin Dashboard Before Chasing Channel ROAS
cards.summary: Track daily contribution margin as the closest daily proxy for cash flow, and keep channel-level ROAS at the bottom of your metric hierarchy.
cards.use_when: Setting up daily reporting or deciding which number your media buyer, email manager and ops team should optimize toward.

cards.title: Use a Returns Accrual So January Dashboards Don't Freeze Your Ad Spend
cards.summary: Accrue estimated returns to the month of purchase instead of letting Shopify's processed-returns reporting make post-holiday efficiency look broken.
cards.use_when: Reading January or post-promo MER while platform dashboards include December returns, and deciding whether to pull back media.

cards.title: Forecast Revenue from Actions, Not Extrapolated Ratios
cards.summary: Build financial forecasts from the marketing calendar of specific actions (launches, promos, email/SMS sends, PR moments) because revenue without an action is not real.
cards.use_when: Building next quarter's revenue plan or reviewing a finance-built forecast that assumes spend up 50% with CAC flat.

cards.title: Reduce Single-Brand Outliers with Cross-Brand Benchmarks
cards.summary: When your own data is too short or volatile to forecast, regress your performance against comparable brands instead of extrapolating an outlier period.
cards.use_when: Forecasting after a breakout year, a shock year, or with under two years of clean data.

cards.title: Engineering Four Peaks a Year to Arbitrage Static Ad Inventory
cards.summary: Create four quarterly demand peaks with cultural or narrative hooks so your conversion rate rises while CPMs stay flat.
cards.use_when: Planning your annual merchandising and campaign calendar to break reliance on BFCM and one seasonal peak.

cards.title: Make Charity or Cause Peaks Work as a New-Customer Engine
cards.summary: Give up margin on a cause-driven drop to acquire a new customer file, then harvest it with the next major peak.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to run a cause or sponsorship moment that generates no contribution margin.

cards.title: Segment SKUs with the Product MVP Matrix and Four SKU Types
cards.summary: Classify every SKU as Champion, Growth Driver, Hidden Gem or Underperformer and assign capital and spend accordingly.
cards.use_when: Doing quarterly assortment review, deciding where to add media spend, or deciding what to liquidate for cash.

cards.title: De-Risk New Category Expansion with Small-Batch and Pre-Orders
cards.summary: Validate demand for a new category with small-batch runs or pre-orders before committing media budget or large purchase orders.
cards.use_when: Considering expansion into a new product category, license or SKU line beyond your core.

cards.title: Track Active Customer File, Not Cumulative Customers
cards.summary: Amortize repeat revenue against an active-customer base and treat the file as decaying when you stop acquiring.
cards.use_when: Evaluating retention, returning-customer revenue and whether your acquisition engine is actually funding next year's revenue.

cards.title: Use a Spend-and-AMER Model to Forecast New-Customer Revenue
cards.summary: Model the spend–efficiency relationship to predict new-customer revenue at each spend level rather than assuming constant CAC.
cards.use_when: Deciding how far to scale media this quarter or evaluating whether a spend increase is realistic.

cards.title: Incrementality Testing New Channels with DMA Hold-Outs
cards.summary: Establish a channel's true causal effect by splitting comparable DMAs into spend-on and spend-off groups and comparing revenue.
cards.use_when: Adding a new channel or a new spend level beyond your core platform and needing a defensible effect estimate.

cards.title: Align Attribution with What the Ad Platform Actually Optimizes For
cards.summary: Report however you like, but ensure you pass a signal back to the platform that matches the number you actually care about.
cards.use_when: Choosing an attribution model and setting conversion optimizations for Meta, Google or TikTok campaigns targeting new-customer revenue.

cards.title: Single-Channel Focus Below $10M Revenue
cards.summary: For younger ecommerce brands, stay concentrated in one platform instead of spreading media across channels.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to launch a second or third paid channel with a lean team and a sub-$10M business.

cards.title: Create for Your Audience's Audience
cards.summary: Design content and ads that make your customer look good when they share them, so identity drives organic distribution.
cards.use_when: Briefing creative or PR before a launch, drop or peak, when you need shareable assets rather than incremental hook iterations.

cards.title: Map the Full Marketing Calendar as Annotated Events
cards.summary: Build a single annotated calendar of every email, SMS, ad, promotion, launch, PR moment and site change so cause and effect become visible.
cards.use_when: Investigating why revenue or efficiency moved in a period, or building the event-effect model used in forecasting.

cards.title: Broaden Media Measurement as You Add Distribution Channels
cards.summary: Measure Meta and YouTube effect on both .com and Amazon via incrementality studies so channel expansion doesn't trigger a false signal to cut spend.
cards.use_when: When Amazon, retail, or marketplace revenue is growing but your .com ROAS is falling and you're considering pulling back on Meta or YouTube spend.

cards.title: Channel Playbook by Revenue Stage
cards.summary: Scale your channel mix to your stage: sub-$10M brands stay Meta-first, $10-100M brands expand into Amazon, TikTok Shop, and upper-funnel media.
cards.use_when: When deciding which sales channels and ad platforms to add next, based on current annual revenue.

cards.title: Amazon Ads and Branded Search as Defensive Tax
cards.summary: Amazon ads and Google branded search defend existing demand rather than create it, and their margin cost rises as category competition increases.
cards.use_when: When deciding how much to budget for Amazon Sponsored Products, Google branded search, or defensive keyword bidding.

cards.title: Four Quarter Accounting: Break Your P&L into Four Buckets
cards.summary: Review only cost of delivery, CAC, opex, and profit each month to find which bucket eats your profit and where to create leverage.
cards.use_when: When your P&L feels unreadable and you need a simple recurring view to find margin problems in the store's finances.

cards.title: Shipping and Cost of Delivery Targets
cards.summary: Track net shipping cost and product cost explicitly, aiming for delivery costs of 30-40% of revenue, because hidden shipping losses quietly kill stores.
cards.use_when: When pricing shipping, evaluating free-shipping thresholds, or auditing fulfillment and 3PL costs.

cards.title: CAC Percentage Depends on LTV Model and Stage
cards.summary: High-LTV brands see marketing as a percent of revenue fall over time; low-LTV hard goods must sustain 40-50%+ marketing spend.
cards.use_when: When setting marketing budget as a percentage of revenue, or evaluating whether your CAC is out of line.

cards.title: Aged Inventory Tiers and Liquidation Funnels
cards.summary: Tier inventory A-D, and liquidate slow stock through unlisted funnels with lower efficiency targets rather than letting cash decay on shelves.
cards.use_when: When you have aging SKUs sitting in the warehouse and need to decide whether to discount, liquidate, or hold.

cards.title: Sync Demand Creation with Inventory Position
cards.summary: Match ad spend to days-of-inventory on your best SKUs: raise efficiency expectations or pause when you're about to sell through, so you maximize marginal value per batch.
cards.use_when: When your media buyer is pushing your best sellers and you want to avoid stockouts or waste marginal margin.

cards.title: Vendor Terms and Cost-of-Capital Arbitrage
cards.summary: Negotiate net terms using each partner's cost of capital and cash needs — pay more margin for longer terms, or take on consignment over dropshipping and full inventory ownership.
cards.use_when: When negotiating supplier, agency, or software contracts and choosing between dropshipping, buying inventory, or consignment.

cards.title: Turn Liquidation and Discount Levers into Cash for New Bets
cards.summary: Whatever the liquidation method, the objective is to convert dead stock to cash fast and make a new bet — never pay to store inventory with no sell plan.
cards.use_when: When deciding whether to hold, discount, or dump inventory that has no active selling plan.

cards.title: Menu of Growth Channels Beyond Meta and Amazon
cards.summary: Add channels per their role: AppLovin and gaming ad networks as incremental new-customer sources, CTV tied to moments where broad distribution can capture the value.
cards.use_when: When selecting the next paid platform to test after Meta and Google.

cards.title: CTV as a Complement to Broad Distribution and Moments
cards.summary: Deploy CTV when you have multiple places for viewers to buy, and align airtime with cultural peaks to amplify demand rather than run it standalone.
cards.use_when: When planning a CTV campaign and deciding whether your channel mix can support it.

cards.title: Four Quarter Accounting vs Cash Flow: Tradeoffs Are Purposeful
cards.summary: Profitability and cash flow are different games — knowingly sacrifice gross margin or P&L efficiency when it accelerates cash and optionality.
cards.use_when: When weighing a decision that hurts P&L margin but improves cash position, such as liquidation, longer-term vendor deals, or consignment.

cards.title: Constraint as a Growth Superpower
cards.summary: A hard CAC/ROAS ceiling forces creative problem-solving — storytelling, creative, channel expansion, product development — instead of buying growth with efficiency.
cards.use_when: When your media team keeps asking to raise the CAC ceiling or lower ROAS targets to hit growth goals.

cards.title: Ecommerce Is a Low-Opex Model — Track Revenue per Employee
cards.summary: Winning ecommerce runs a lean fixed cost base (~10-15% opex benchmark), and your fixed dollars of opex should fall year over year even as revenue grows.
cards.use_when: When auditing team size, software costs, and overhead, or planning AI/tooling investments to raise output per person.

cards.title: Don't Let .com Efficiency Reports Choke the Whole-Enterprise Engine
cards.summary: When media drives all channels but is measured only on .com, declining .com efficiency signals a pullback that stalls growth of the entire business.
cards.use_when: When reviewing .com performance and feeling pressure to cut spend on Meta/YouTube because only .com attribution looks soft.

cards.title: Use Hard Constraints to Force Creative Problem-Solving
cards.summary: Set an immovable cap on CAC or blended efficiency and refuse to lower the standard, forcing the team to innovate around it.
cards.use_when: Setting acquisition targets, media budgets, or efficiency goals for a store's marketing team, or deciding whether to relax a CAC/ROAS target when performance degrades.

cards.title: Know When a Category's Profit Has Been Competed Away
cards.summary: If a product category is saturated by the best global brands, growth must come from category expansion, not from squeezing more ad efficiency.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to push for more paid-media efficiency on an existing hero category or to invest in new product categories.

cards.title: Treat Product Development as Growth Marketing
cards.summary: Growth is as much category expansion and product development as media spend; the CEO is the real head of growth and a capital allocator.
cards.use_when: Deciding where to allocate next year's investment budget between media, R&D, and new product development.

cards.title: Build a Product Matrix of Media Spend vs. Unit Velocity
cards.summary: Map every SKU's unit sales against the media dollars allocated to it to find hidden gems, champions, growth drivers, and underperformers.
cards.use_when: Prioritizing which SKUs to invest media behind, expand creatively, or liquidate.
